# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterized by delayed opacification of epicardial coronary arteries in the absence of obstructive coronary artery disease [1]. First systematically described by Tambe and colleagues in 1972, the condition has since been recognized as a distinct clinical and pathophysiological entity rather than a benign incidental finding [2]. Patients frequently present with recurrent chest pain, and CSFP may account for a meaningful proportion of admissions for acute coronary syndromes with non-obstructed coronary arteries [3]. This review summarizes the current understanding of the epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, clinical implications, and management of CSFP.

## Definition and Diagnosis

The diagnosis of CSFP rests on quantitative angiographic assessment, most commonly using the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count developed by Gibson et al., which provides a reproducible measure of coronary flow [4]. The corrected TIMI frame count is widely applied, with values exceeding the mean by two standard deviations indicating slow flow [5]. CSFP is typically defined as a TIMI frame count greater than two standard deviations above the established normal range for a given vessel in the absence of significant stenosis [6]. The phenomenon must be distinguished from the no-reflow phenomenon, which occurs after reperfusion therapy, and from secondary slow flow related to ectasia or coronary spasm [7].

## Epidemiology

CSFP is reported in approximately 1–7% of patients undergoing coronary angiography for suspected ischemia [8]. It demonstrates a male predominance and tends to affect relatively younger patients, with smoking identified as a frequent risk factor [9]. Metabolic disturbances, including features of the metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance, have also been associated with the condition [10].

## Pathophysiology

The pathophysiology of CSFP remains incompletely understood and is likely multifactorial. Microvascular dysfunction is the most widely supported mechanism, with elevated microvascular resistance demonstrated in affected vessels [11]. Endothelial dysfunction plays a central role, evidenced by reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and impaired flow-mediated dilation in patients with CSFP [12]. Histopathological studies of myocardial biopsies have demonstrated small-vessel abnormalities including endothelial swelling, fibromuscular hyperplasia, and luminal narrowing [13]. Subclinical diffuse atherosclerosis, detectable by intravascular ultrasound even in angiographically normal segments, has been proposed as a contributing substrate [14].

Inflammation appears to be intimately involved, with elevated levels of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and other inflammatory markers reported in affected patients [15]. Oxidative stress and an imbalance between endothelin-1 and nitric oxide have been implicated as well [16]. Increased platelet activation and altered platelet indices, such as mean platelet volume, suggest a prothrombotic milieu [17]. Disturbances in autonomic regulation and abnormal coronary vasomotor tone have additionally been described [18].

## Clinical Presentation and Prognosis

The dominant clinical feature is recurrent angina, which may occur both at rest and on exertion and frequently leads to repeated hospitalizations and diagnostic procedures [19]. Although traditionally regarded as benign, CSFP is increasingly linked to adverse outcomes. It has been associated with myocardial ischemia documented by perfusion imaging and with impaired left ventricular function on advanced echocardiographic assessment [20]. Importantly, CSFP has been implicated in life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, and electrocardiographic markers such as prolonged QT dispersion and increased Tp-e interval have been reported [21]. Recurrent acute coronary events have also been documented during long-term follow-up [22]. Quality of life is often substantially impaired in this population [23].

## Management

There is no universally accepted treatment for CSFP, and therapy remains largely empirical and symptom-directed [24]. Dipyridamole, through its adenosine-mediated vasodilatory and anti-inflammatory effects, has shown benefit in improving coronary flow and reducing symptoms [25]. Calcium channel blockers, particularly mibefradil and other agents, have been studied for their ability to reduce TIMI frame counts and angina frequency [26]. Nebivolol, a beta-blocker with nitric oxide-potentiating properties, has improved both flow parameters and endothelial function in clinical studies [27]. Statins may exert favorable effects through their anti-inflammatory and endothelial-stabilizing actions, independent of lipid lowering [28]. Nitric oxide donors such as nicorandil have demonstrated improvement in coronary flow in small trials [29]. Lifestyle modification, especially smoking cessation and management of metabolic risk factors, remains an essential component of care [30].

## Conclusion

CSFP is a distinct entity defined by delayed coronary opacification without obstructive disease. Microvascular dysfunction, endothelial impairment, inflammation, and subclinical atherosclerosis underlie its pathophysiology. Though once considered benign, accumulating evidence links it to ischemia, arrhythmia, and impaired quality of life. Further large-scale studies are needed to standardize diagnosis and establish evidence-based therapies.
